newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition protests on election day. [CORRECTED 18:17 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition protests on election day. [CORRECTED 18:17 GMT]

text.p: Tens of thousands of opposition supporters began marching through the centre of Belgrade in freezing weather on Wednesday to campaign against a re-run of local elections they say they won.

The marchers moved towards the state parliament building, retracing the route similar protests have taken each day since local electoral commissions cancelled opposition victories in local elections 10 days ago.

Zoran Djindjic, a key leader in the opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) coalition which won elections in 15 (corrects from 5) of the 18 biggest towns in Serbia, marched at the head of the column which observers said was bigger than Tuesday's crowd of 40,000.

The march came as voters in the disputed municipalities cast their ballots for the third round of polling. The demonstration took place in defiance of electoral laws which prohibit political meetings on polling day.
Polling was scheduled to begin at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) and continue until 8 p.m. (1900 GMT). No early estimates of the turnout were available.
Zajedno had called for a boycott in Belgrade of Wednesday's voting, which it called a "farce" devised to seal results of poll fraud.

The march moved to the state television studios and then to the Politika newspaper offices -- both controlled by President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist Party -- where protesters hurled rocks and abuse at the buildings.
The crowd smashed dozens of windows in both buildings, where opposition supporters had earlier used only eggs and paint bombs to deface the walls.
Firecrackers also exploded on the fringes of the demonstration, which witnesses said appeared to be more aggressive and vocal than earlier marches, although no violence was reported.
Later Djindjic appealed for restraint, and called on his followers to maintain the pressure on Milosevic.

"Do not break windows, do not throw stones. What we want is victory through the will of the people," he told the crowd. "We will be here every day until the chains break, until the ice melts. Serbia is being defended here."
Several thousand university students, who have effectively shut down Belgrade faculties, marched through the city centre again earlier on Wednesday in support of the opposition demands.
The students jeered at police with riot gear deployed along the route in a largely peaceful march.
Djindjic said the protests showed ordinary people were fed up with Milosevic's authoritarian rule and were eager for democratic reforms that have swept across Eastern Europe.
The city electoral commission has warned the opposition to respect a law which bans campaigning for the last two days before voting.

The Zajedno coalition dismissed the warning and predicted a high turnout to protests in towns across the country as supporters realised Milosevic's Socialists would not concede defeat even at the municipal level.
In the industrial town of Nis, opposition spokesman Biserka Zivkovic told Reuters that a crowd of 15,000 had joined another protest in what has become a "daily routine".
